c.tagline: Nigeria's carnival city on the Cross River, green, historic and welcoming.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow taxis and shared drop cabs work on negotiated fares, so agree the price before setting off; yellow keke (tricycles) handle short hops cheaply. Bolt operates in the city, while Uber coverage is limited.

emergency.note: 112 is Nigeria's national emergency number; response can be unreliable, so hotel security, the state's own security outfit and private clinics are often the faster first call.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Avoid the waterfront and poorly lit outskirts after dark, and rural Cross River roads beyond the city due to kidnapping risk.
Watch for pickpockets and bag snatching around Watt Market and crowded motor parks, especially during Carnival season.

hood_desc: A secure, well-planned central estate of interconnected roads, parks and hotels, home to influential residents and much of the city's mid-range accommodation; a convenient, safe base.
The lively Marian Road corridor lined with restaurants, bars, malls and nightlife; central and buzzing, best for travelers who want dining and going out on their doorstep.
An up-and-coming upscale area of new gated homes near the Nigerian Army Amphibious Training School, quieter and leafier north of the centre; suited to longer, calmer stays.
The historic waterfront quarter of Duke Town, with the Slave History Museum, colonial churches and the Marina; steeped in the trans-Atlantic slave-trade past and best for sights along the river.

The Tinapa Business & Leisure Resort complex on the Calabar River about 9 km north of Duke Town, in Odukpani LGA: a purpose-built free-trade and film-studio site with a lakeside hotel, water park and open lakefront. Quiet and self-contained, and only worth basing yourself in if the resort itself is the reason you came.

water.note: Drink bottled or properly filtered water only.

transit.hours: Taxis and keke run from early morning to late evening; after dark a booked cab or hotel car is the safest option.
transit.note: Calabar has no rail, tram or formal city bus system. Shared yellow taxis (drop cabs) and yellow keke tricycles are the main way around, with Bolt and limited Uber for door-to-door trips.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (naira) and negotiated; keke hops cost small change, while ride-hailing apps take cards or cash. There is no transit card.

bus: Long-distance coaches to Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt (ABC Transport, God is Good Motors, Cross Lines)
Shared taxis to Ikom, Obudu and Uyo
ferry: Passenger boats and speedboats across the Cross River estuary to Oron and creek communities

transit.m: Taxi to the city centre (10-15 min)
Bolt ride-hail into town when drivers are available

tip.r: ~10% or a small 'dash' for good service; tipping porters and drivers is appreciated.

food.name: Edikang ikong
food.desc: Calabar's most famous soup: pumpkin leaves and waterleaf cooked down with palm oil, dried fish, periwinkles and beef, eaten with pounded yam or eba.

places.name: Native Delicacies Restaurant
places.note: Specialises in Efik home cooking; a standard reference point for edikang ikong in the city.

places.name: Freddy's Restaurant
places.note: Long-established Calabar institution that plates local soups alongside continental dishes.

places.name: Mustard Seed Restaurant
places.note: Roomy indoor and garden seating, popular with families for full traditional soup plates.

food.name: Afang soup
food.desc: Shredded afang (ukazi) leaves with waterleaf, palm oil, smoked fish, snails and assorted meat; richer and darker than edikang ikong.

places.name: Native Delicacies Restaurant
places.note: Cooks afang the Efik way with generous snail and periwinkle; go early on weekends.

places.name: The Home Restaurant and Lounge
places.note: Local and international menu in a comfortable setting; reliable afang and swallow.

places.name: Marian Road bukas
places.note: Roadside local kitchens along Marian serve afang at working-lunch prices all day.

food.name: Ekpang nkukwo
food.desc: Grated cocoyam and water yam wrapped in cocoyam leaves and steamed in palm oil stock with dried fish and periwinkle; a labour-intensive Efik treasure.

places.name: Native Delicacies Restaurant
places.note: One of the few restaurants that makes ekpang nkukwo properly; often available at weekends.

places.name: Watt Market food stalls
places.note: Market cooks sell ekpang by the wrap; the best place to eat it as locals do.

places.name: Mustard Seed Restaurant
places.note: Carries ekpang on its traditional menu; call ahead as it sells out quickly.

food.name: Fisherman soup (efere ndek iyak)
food.desc: Peppery riverine broth loaded with fresh fish, crayfish, prawns and periwinkle from the Cross River, eaten with garri or on its own as a pepper soup.

places.name: Marina Resort waterfront
places.note: Riverside eateries in the marina complex do seafood soups with the river in view.

places.name: Freddy's Restaurant
places.note: Dependable kitchen for fresh seafood soups when river catch is in.

places.name: Native Delicacies Restaurant
places.note: Traditional fisherman soup with generous seafood, well spiced rather than merely hot.

food.name: Editan and atama soups
food.desc: Two bitter-leaf cousins: editan, sharp and medicinal, and atama, scented with atama leaf and banga palm fruit; both classic Efik and Ibibio Sunday soups.

places.name: Native Delicacies Restaurant
places.note: Rotates editan and atama through the week alongside the better-known soups.

places.name: Watt Market food stalls
places.note: Market cooks make atama with fresh banga; cheap, authentic and busy at midday.

places.name: E3 Restaurant
places.note: Blends local soups with an international menu in the old colonial quarter.

food.name: Palm wine (mmin efik)
food.desc: Milky sap tapped from raffia or oil palms, drunk fresh and sweet in the morning or sharper and more alcoholic by evening.

places.name: Marina Resort waterfront
places.note: Open-air riverside bars serve fresh palm wine in calabashes with pepper soup.

places.name: Watt Market
places.note: Tappers sell by the bottle each morning; buy early for the sweetest wine.

places.name: Palm wine joints, Etta Agbor Road
places.note: Cluster of casual evening bars where palm wine is drunk with grilled fish and nkwobi.

food.name: Zobo and chapman
food.desc: Zobo is chilled hibiscus steeped with ginger, cloves and pineapple; chapman is the Nigerian bar staple of Fanta, blackcurrant, bitters and cucumber.

places.name: Freddy's Restaurant
places.note: Full bar with a well-made chapman, a Calabar dining-out ritual.

places.name: The Home Restaurant and Lounge
places.note: Lounge setting with cold zobo and mocktails; good for an evening without alcohol.

places.name: Watt Market drink sellers
places.note: Home-made zobo sold in chilled bottles for a few naira; ask for less sugar.

landmarks: Slave History Museum
Set at Marina Resort beside the Calabar River, this sobering museum documents the transatlantic slave trade through shackles, artifacts, and dioramas at a former trading point.
National Museum Calabar (Old Residency)
Housed in a prefabricated 1884 British colonial residency shipped from Glasgow, its exhibits chronicle Old Calabar's palm-oil trade, missionaries, and Efik royal history.
Marina Resort
Calabar's breezy riverside leisure hub combines boat cruises, a carousel, and waterfront lounges with sweeping views across the broad, mangrove-fringed Calabar River.
Drill Ranch (Pandrillus Drill Monkey Sanctuary)
A pioneering primate rehabilitation center in town where visitors meet endangered drill monkeys and chimpanzees rescued from the bushmeat and pet trades.
Kwa Falls
A short drive north, the Kwa River plunges through a lush rainforest gorge into a natural pool, one of Cross River State's prettiest escapes.
Duke Town Presbyterian Church
Founded by Scottish missionaries in 1846, this historic hilltop church anchors Duke Town and witnessed the earliest chapters of Christianity in southeastern Nigeria.
Mary Slessor's Tomb
The grave of the beloved Scottish missionary who ended twin killings in the region draws pilgrims to a cross-marked memorial overlooking old Calabar.
Tinapa Business and Leisure Resort
An ambitious free-trade zone and resort complex on the Calabar River, its waterpark, studios, and shopping emporiums showcase Nigeria's grandest leisure experiment.
Cross River National Park (Oban Division)
Day-trippable from the city, this vast rainforest sanctuary shelters gorillas, forest elephants, and dazzling butterflies within one of Africa's oldest jungles.
Millennium Park and Calabar Carnival Route
The landscaped green heart of Nigeria's cleanest city, whose boulevards explode each December with Africa's biggest street party, the Calabar Carnival.

train.note: Calabar has never been connected to Nigeria's rail network - the eastern narrow-gauge line runs well inland through Port Harcourt, Enugu and Makurdi, and the long-promised Calabar-Lagos coastal railway remains unbuilt. The nearest place to pick up a Nigerian Railway Corporation train is Port Harcourt, several hours away by road, and even there services are irregular. See https://nrc.gov.ng/ for what the national network actually runs. There are no international trains from Nigeria at all.

bus.note: Coaches from Lagos (12+ hours), Abuja, Port Harcourt and Enugu pull into each operator's own terminal rather than a single station; ABC Transport (https://www.abctransport.com/) has a Calabar terminal and sells online, while Young Shall Grow, Peace Mass Transit, AKTC and Transit Favor are cash-at-the-park. No scheduled coach crosses into Cameroon: the overland route is by shared taxi or minibus to Ikom and the Mfum/Ekok border post, then Cameroonian bush taxis on to Mamfe and Bamenda, a slow crossing that needs a Cameroonian visa arranged in advance.

intl.to: Limbe & Idenau (Cameroon) - motorised passenger boats from the Marina/Calabar Beach jetty
intl.op: licensed local boat operators, tickets bought at the jetty (no online booking)

intl.to: Oron (Nigeria) - fast boats across the Cross River estuary from Calabar Beach jetty
intl.op: local boat operators, tickets bought at the jetty (no online booking)

ferry.note: Calabar sits on the Calabar River a few kilometres upstream of the Cross River estuary, and passenger boats leave from the Marina/Calabar Beach jetty rather than the commercial Calabar Port complex. Cross-border boats to the Cameroonian coast around Limbe and Idenau carry people and vehicles and take several hours in open water; Cameroonian visas have sometimes been issued on board, but do not count on it. The much shorter hop across the estuary to Oron in Akwa Ibom State runs through the day and saves a long road detour. Sea conditions and safety standards are poor in the rainy season, roughly May to October.

full.name: Agbokim Waterfalls
full.blurb: Seven-stream waterfall cascading through rainforest near the Cameroon border, one of Cross River State's natural landmarks.

full.name: Ibeno Beach
full.blurb: One of Nigeria's longest sand beaches, a quiet stretch of coast in neighboring Akwa Ibom State.
